summary: Builds on RFC 1006, which supplies the ISO transport service over TCP, to show how the OSI session, presentation, and application layers can be run on top of it. This lets OSI applications work on TCP/IP-based internets.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1085 offers a small way to run OSI applications over TCP/IP. Instead of building the full OSI session and presentation layers, the memo says to agree in advance on everything that would otherwise be negotiated, and then send the application's data objects directly over the connection. That keeps the software a program needs down to three small modules.

questions: iso presentation services over tcp ip
how to run osi applications on tcp ip
how does rfc 1085 emulate the presentation service
subtitle: A pared-down way to run OSI applications on TCP/IP without building the whole OSI stack.

tldr.problem: OSI applications need the OSI session, presentation and application services to work, and RFC 1006 showed how to put the OSI transport service on top of TCP. But in constrained environments it is impractical to implement all that underlying infrastructure just to run one application.
tldr.mechanism: The memo emulates the small part of the OSI presentation service that the association control and remote operations service elements need, by serialising ASN.1 objects straight onto a TCP connection. The transfer syntax and the presentation contexts are fixed in advance, so nothing has to be negotiated, and a dispatch, a serialisation and a network module make up the whole implementation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1085 proposes a standard for the Internet community but the RFC Editor's index gives it no status category, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The memo notes that an OSI application built this way can be moved to an RFC 1006 environment with no modifications.

today: RFC 1085 proposes a standard for the Internet community, but the RFC Editor's index gives it no status category, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The memo's own remarks note that an OSI application built this way can be moved to an RFC 1006 based environment with no modifications, and that the method was meant to stay small rather than grow towards the full ISO presentation protocol.

sections.title: Why a Lighter Way to Run OSI Applications
sections.content:
RFC 1006 describes a mechanism for providing the ISO transport service on top of TCP and IP. Once that method is applied, real ISO applications can be implemented on TCP/IP-based internets by implementing the OSI session, presentation and application services on top of the transport service access point provided over TCP. Although straightforward, there are environments where the richness of the OSI application layer is desired but implementing the underlying OSI infrastructure, the presentation, session and transport services on top of TCP, is impractical. This memo describes an approach for providing streamlined support of OSI application services over TCP/IP-based internets for such constrained environments.

The mechanism is targeted at a particular class of OSI applications: those whose application context contains only an Association Control Service Element, which manages associations between application entities, and a Remote Operations Service Element, which orchestrates the invocation of total operations between application entities. A Directory Services Element is assumed to be used by the application entity, but only in a very limited sense. The mechanism is not applicable to entities whose application context is more extensive, for example one containing a Reliable Transfer Service Element, although it could be modified to support additional elements. Such extensions would, at this time, merely defeat the purpose of providing the minimal software infrastructure needed to run the majority of OSI applications.

The motivation came from a requirement to run the ISO Common Management Information Protocol in TCP/IP-based internets, since in its current definition CMIP uses precisely the application service elements provided for here. It may be desirable to offer CMIP users a quality of service different from the one offered by a connection with a high level of reliability, which would permit reduced use of connection-related resources, and this memo proposes a mechanism to implement that less robust and less costly quality of service.

The memo's own remarks note that if one really wanted to implement ISO applications in a TCP/IP-based network, the method of RFC 1006 is the preferred one, and that in a constrained environment this memo proposes an alternative. An OSI application realised this way can be moved directly to an RFC 1006 based environment with no modifications. As more presentation service functionality is added, the method proposed here would begin to approximate the ISO presentation protocol, which is contrary to the key motivation, so featurism must be avoided at all costs.
sections.plainLanguage: The full OSI stack is a lot of software to write when all an application really needs is a way to exchange structured objects with a remote program. This memo keeps only the part that the association and remote operation elements use, and leaves out everything else. The trade-off is stated plainly in the memo's remarks: an application written this way can be moved to the fuller approach later without changes.

sections.title: The Approach: ASN.1 Objects Over TCP
sections.content:
The approach relies on a set of architectural nuances: the TCP is a stream-oriented transport protocol; ASN.1 objects, when represented as a stream of octets, are self-delimiting; the ISO presentation service permits the exchange of ASN.1 objects; the ACSE and ROSE require the connection establishment facility, the connection termination facility and the information transfer facility, the P-DATA service only; and the majority of the parameters used by the services that provide these facilities can be hard-wired to avoid negotiation.

Together these suggest that a cheap emulation of the ISO presentation services could be implemented by simply serialising ASN.1 objects over a TCP connection, and that is exactly what the memo proposes. The overall composition is a client and a server, each implementing the protocol described in the memo, each offering a presentation service interface to its user and a TCP interface below. The essential features of the ISO presentation service are maintained while using a protocol entirely different from the one given in ISO 8823.

Each box contains three modules. A dispatch module provides the presentation services interface. A serialisation module holds a serializer, which takes an ASN.1 object and applies the encoding rules of ISO 8825 to produce a stream of octets, and a de-serializer, which performs the inverse operation. A network module manages the TCP connection. The flow of data is that the user hands an object to the dispatch module, which passes it to the serializer through an input queue; the serializer's output goes through an output queue to the network. In the other direction the network's input queue feeds the de-serializer, whose output queue feeds the dispatch module.

The ISO presentation layer is concerned primarily with the negotiation of transfer syntaxes in addition to the transformation to and from transfer syntax. With this mechanism no negotiation component is employed. The memo specifies the fixed contexts that exist over each presentation connection offered, and further specifies other constants used in order to eliminate the need for presentation layer negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole mechanism is: turn each application data object into bytes and send them. The trick that makes it work is that ASN.1 objects say where they end, so the receiver can find the boundary of each one in the byte stream without any extra framing. Three modules do the work: one that hands objects between the application and the network, one that turns objects into bytes and back, and one that manages the connection.

sections.title: The Fixed Parameters
sections.content:
A presentation address is interpreted as an ordered tuple containing one or more network addresses, a transport selector, a session selector and a presentation selector, each selector being an uninterpreted octet string of possibly zero length. The mechanism ignores the values of these selectors, except that the value of the presentation selector is preserved by the provider. A network address is interpreted as containing a 32-bit IP address, a set indicating which transport services are available at that IP address, currently only two members, TCP and UDP, each possibly carrying an intensity of possibly present or definitely present, and a 16-bit port number. As a consequence, any application entity residing in the network can be identified by its network address.

The presentation context list holds one or more presentation contexts, each with a presentation context identifier, an integer, an abstract syntax name, an object identifier, and an abstract transfer name, an object identifier. The range of values these components may take is severely restricted: exactly two contexts are defined, one for association control and the other for the specific application service element carried as remote operations APDUs. In a result list a fourth component appears, an acceptance indicator saying whether the context was accepted by both the service provider and the remote peer, with a brief reason such as abstract syntax not supported if it was not accepted. The memo offers an analogy for the novice reader: the abstract syntax notation defines the vocabulary of a language, listing the words that can be spoken, while the abstract transfer notation defines the pronunciation.

User data passes through the presentation service interface as ASN.1 objects in a locally defined form, each associated with a presentation context identifier that distinguishes the context the data is intended for. Exactly one of two contexts must always be used, either the value for the ACSE presentation context or the value for ROSE. Quality of service is a collection of elements, and only one is interpreted, transport-mapping, which takes one of two values, tcp-based or udp-based, also referred to as high-quality or low-quality. Implementations of this memo always indicate that session service version 2 has been negotiated.

The memo also assumes and specifies a minimal Directory service capability. The Directory Services Element provides two mappings: a service name is mapped into an application entity title, a global handle on the service, and the application entity title is mapped onto a presentation address. The service name for an OSI application entity using this mechanism is a designator and a qualifier separated by a hyphen, where the designator is a string denoting either a domain name or a 32-bit IP address and the qualifier denotes the type of application entity desired, for example gonzo.twg.com-mgmtinfobase. The presentation address then carries the 32-bit IP address resolved from the designator, the set of available transport services, the 16-bit port number resolved from the qualifier using the Assigned Numbers document, and optionally a presentation selector. The simplest implementation uses the Domain Name System to map the designator to an IP address and a local table derived from the Assigned Numbers document for the port number.
sections.plainLanguage: Because nothing is negotiated, every value has to be fixed in advance, and the memo does that explicitly. There are exactly two presentation contexts, one for setting up the association and one for the application's own messages. The transfer syntax is always the basic ASN.1 encoding rules. The transport is chosen in advance as either TCP or UDP. And a service is found by a name of the form host-service, which a directory lookup turns into an IP address and a port number.

sections.title: Choosing TCP or UDP
sections.content:
The quality of service parameter of the P-CONNECT service selects the underlying transport service. If transport-mapping is tcp-based, the presentation provider uses TCP; if it is udp-based, the provider uses UDP instead. Very few transport-level facilities are placed on top of the UDP service, and it is not the intent of the memo to re-invent the facilities in TCP. The memo is emphatic that low-quality means low-quality.

Because UDP is a packet-oriented protocol, the role of the serialisation module is slightly redefined. For the serializer, each top-level ASN.1 object placed on the input queue forms a single UDP datagram on the output queue that is given to the network. For the de-serializer, each UDP datagram placed on the input queue from the network forms a single top-level ASN.1 object placed on the output queue. The term top-level ASN.1 object refers to the protocol data units being exchanged by the presentation providers.

The memo permits the choice of two transport protocols, TCP or UDP, and explains that as experience is gained and other transport protocols are deployed, such as VMTP, future incarnations would permit them. That is a three step process: the set of transport services defined for the network address is updated, a corresponding value is added to the range of the transport-mapping quality of service element, and the following sections of the memo are modified accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: The two transports are not treated equally, and the memo says so. With TCP the objects are simply written into the byte stream. With UDP each object becomes one datagram, so a large object will not fit and the receiver gets nothing if the datagram is lost, since nothing is retransmitted. The choice is fixed in advance, in the quality of service parameter.

sections.title: Opening, Closing and Carrying Data
sections.content:
The connection establishment facility consists of one service, P-CONNECT, used to bring two identified application entities into communication. Its successful use results in a presentation connection with an initial defined context set being established between them. It is a confirmed service whose effects are sequenced and non-destructive. If the udp-based service is selected, a presentation connection is formed which should be used infrequently and will have minimal reliability characteristics. For the purposes of this memo, P-CONNECT requests TCP or UDP resources, builds a fixed defined context set, and exchanges initial user data.

The parameters have fixed interpretations. The calling presentation address may, in practice, be replaced by a local rule that picks an ephemeral address. The called presentation address may carry more than one network address in the request, while the indication carries only the one actually used. The responding presentation address is identical to the called address of the indication. Multiple defined contexts is always TRUE. The presentation context definition list holds two contexts: presentation context identifier 1 with an abstract syntax specific to the application and the transfer name iso asn.1 abstract transfer 1.0.8825, and identifier 3 with the abstract syntax acse pci version 1, 2.2.1.0.0, and the same transfer name, for use with the DIS version of association control; if the IS version is used, identifier 3 carries acse pci version 1, 2.2.1.0.1, with the transfer name asn.1 basic encoding, 2.1.1. The context result list is identical with the acceptance indicator for both contexts set to accepted. The default context name is none and the default context result is not applicable. Presentation requirements are none, because the kernel functional unit is always used, and session requirements are full duplex. The session connection identifier has a format that the memo mandates, holding user data as a local string encoded as a T.61 string using ASN.1, common data as a universal time encoding using ASN.1, and optional additional data as a T.61 string. The user data is a single ASN.1 object, the appropriate A-ASSOCIATE PDU, carried in presentation context 3, and the result is one of acceptance, user-rejection, provider-rejection transient or provider-rejection permanent.

The connection termination facility consists of three services. P-RELEASE gives the service user access to a negotiated release facility, has effects that are sequenced and non-destructive, and either user may request it, though a collision invokes a provider-initiated abort. It waits for the serialisation module to drain, sends release user data and releases the TCP or UDP resources; if the udp-based service is selected, any data in transit may be discarded. P-U-ABORT lets either user force the release of the connection at any time and have the correspondent informed, without requiring the agreement of both users; it flushes the serialisation module, sends abort user data and releases the resources. P-P-ABORT is the provider's way of indicating termination for reasons internal to the provider, with an integer provider reason such as invalid PPDU parameter, unexpected PPDU, unrecognised PPDU or specified reason.

The information transfer facility consists of many services, but only one, P-DATA, is provided, giving the service user a data transfer capability with sequenced and non-destructive effects. Its user data is a single ASN.1 object, a remote operations APDU, carried in presentation context 1. If the udp-based service is selected there is an upper bound on the size of the serialised ASN.1 objects that may be transmitted, imposed by UDP at 65536 octets, and as a practical matter it is probably a good idea to keep datagrams at 536 octets or less.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a connection sends one object, the association request, and fixes the two contexts for the life of the connection. Closing is done in one of three ways: a polite release, an abort by one side, or an abort by the provider when something has gone wrong. Carrying data is one service that sends one object at a time, and over UDP each object has to fit inside a datagram.

sections.title: Elements of Procedure
sections.content:
The service provider is in one of the following states: IDLE, WAIT1, WAIT2, DATA, WAIT3 or WAIT4. The possible events come from the PS-user, such as P-CONNECT.REQUEST, P-CONNECT.RESPONSE, P-RELEASE.REQUEST, P-RELEASE.RESPONSE, P-DATA.REQUEST and P-U-ABORT.REQUEST, and from the network, such as the TCP closing or erroring, the arrival of ConnectRequest, ConnectResponse, ReleaseRequest or ReleaseResponse PDUs, the arrival of UserData or CL-UserData PDUs, the arrival of a user-initiated or provider-initiated Abort PDU, and a timer expiring. The possible actions are the corresponding indications and confirmations to the PS-user, and to the network, opening or closing the TCP connection, sending the PDUs, and setting the timer. Opening and closing the TCP and the CL-UserData PDU and the timer apply to one transport or the other: the TCP actions are for the tcp-based service only, and the CL-UserData PDU and the timer for the udp-based service only.

For the tcp-based service, the provider keeps a local designator for the PS-user, a local designator for a TCP connection, and the state of the connection. An event from the network is matched to a presentation connection by comparing local designators for the TCP connection, and whenever a connection remains in or returns to the IDLE state any associated resources, such as an attachment to a local TCP port, are released. Outgoing PDUs are placed on the input queue for the serializer. If the PDU is not an abort PDU it is simply appended regardless of how many PDUs are queued. If it is an abort PDU and the input queue is non-empty, or the serializer is busy transmitting, the abort PDU is discarded and the serializer is flushed, aborting output in progress. If the queue is empty the abort PDU is appended and a small timer started, and if the timer expires before the PDU has been serialised and transmitted, the serializer is flushed. Whenever the TCP connection is closed or has errored the serializer is flushed, with the single exception of a ReleaseResponse PDU being serialised and transmitted, in which case the connection is not closed until the serializer has finished.

For the udp-based service, the provider keeps the local designators and the state, plus the 32-bit IP address and 16-bit UDP port number of both the initiating and the responding host, the session connection identifier used to establish the connection, a local designator for a UDP endpoint, and a retransmission counter. Matching an incoming event to a connection is done on the basis of addresses, ports and the session connection identifier, so two different presentation connections may differ only in that identifier. If no connection can be found, a vanilla presentation connection may be assumed, initialised to the IDLE state. Outgoing PDUs are serialised and the resulting octets sent as a single UDP datagram.

The state transitions follow a fixed pattern. In the IDLE state, a P-CONNECT.REQUEST makes the provider select an address, attach itself to the port, try to establish a TCP connection if the tcp-based service is chosen, and put a ConnectRequest PDU on the serializer's input queue; for the udp-based service it sets the retransmission counter to a small value, for example 2, and starts a small timer. The provider enters WAIT1. A ConnectRequest PDU received in the IDLE state produces a P-CONNECT.INDICATION and the WAIT2 state, while any other PDU received produces a provider-initiated Abort PDU and leaves the provider in IDLE.

In WAIT1, a ConnectResponse PDU received cancels the timer for the udp-based service; if the PDU indicates rejection the provider issues a negative P-CONNECT.CONFIRMATION and enters IDLE, otherwise a positive confirmation and the DATA state. A user-initiated Abort PDU produces a P-U-ABORT.INDICATION and the IDLE state, and any other PDU produces a provider-initiated Abort PDU, a P-P-ABORT.INDICATION and the IDLE state. When the timer expires the retransmission counter is decremented; if the result is less than or equal to zero the provider issues a negative P-CONNECT.CONFIRMATION and enters IDLE, otherwise another ConnectRequest PDU is queued, the timer started again, and the provider stays in WAIT1.

In WAIT2, a P-CONNECT.RESPONSE puts a ConnectResponse PDU on the queue, and the result parameter decides whether the provider enters IDLE, on user-rejection, or the DATA state, on acceptance. In the DATA state, a P-DATA.REQUEST queues a UserData PDU and the provider stays in DATA; a P-RELEASE.REQUEST queues a ReleaseRequest PDU and the provider enters WAIT3; a UserData PDU received produces a P-DATA.INDICATION and stays in DATA; and a ReleaseRequest PDU received produces a P-RELEASE.INDICATION and the WAIT4 state. In WAIT3, a ReleaseResponse PDU received produces a P-RELEASE.CONFIRMATION and the IDLE state, and an expired timer decrements the retransmission counter, leading to a provider-initiated abort when it reaches zero. In WAIT4, a P-RELEASE.RESPONSE queues a ReleaseResponse PDU and the provider enters IDLE. If the udp-based service is selected, CL-UserData PDUs are exchanged by the provider instead of UserData PDUs.
sections.plainLanguage: The provider is a small state machine with six states. It waits for a connection request, waits for the answer, passes data, then waits for the release to be answered and for the answer to the release. Over TCP the connection itself does the resending; over UDP the provider keeps a retransmission counter and resends the request itself a couple of times before giving up.
